subject: physics
title: Contamination, irradiation and radiation hazards
key_idea: **Irradiation** is exposure to radiation from a source outside the body. **Contamination** is radioactive material on or inside the body. The hazard depends on the type of radiation and the half-life, and precautions limit exposure.

blocks.text: Radiation can reach a person in two different ways. This section covers what each one means and how they differ.

items.meaning: Exposing an object or person to nuclear radiation. The object does not become radioactive.
The unwanted presence of radioactive atoms on or inside an object or person.
Radiation that removes electrons from atoms to make ions. It can damage cells and cause mutations.

items: In irradiation the source is **outside** the object.
Irradiation stops when the source is removed or shielded, or when you move away.
In contamination the radioactive atoms are **on or inside** the object.
Contamination keeps irradiating the person until the atoms are removed or have decayed.

Contamination is radioactive atoms on or inside the object.
Contamination continues until the atoms are removed or have decayed.

blocks.text: Nuclear radiation is ionising. It damages living cells, and the type of radiation changes how dangerous it is.

items: Radiation can **kill cells** and damage tissue.
It can damage DNA and cause **mutations** and cancer.
Radiation can burn the skin.

blocks.text: An alpha source inside the body is much more dangerous. The alpha radiation is absorbed by living tissue and it is highly ionising.

items: Alpha inside the body can damage cells, tissues, organs and DNA.
The risk lasts until the material is removed or excreted.
Ionising radiation damages cells and can cause mutations and cancer.
Alpha is low risk outside the body but highly dangerous inside it.
Beta and gamma are more penetrating, so they can irradiate a person from outside.

blocks.text: Radioactive isotopes have a very wide range of half-lives. The half-life changes how hazardous a source is.

items: For the same number of nuclei, a **short** half-life means a higher activity: more radiation is emitted per second.
So the source with the shorter half-life is the greater hazard at the start.
A **long** half-life means the material stays radioactive, and so stays dangerous, for longer.
Keep a safe distance and handle sources with **tongs**.
Limit the time of exposure.
Use shielding, such as a lead container or a screen.
Wear protective clothing, such as a lead apron, and a radiation badge.
Keep sources in sealed containers and point them away from people.
Limit the dose given to a patient to the smallest that works. Medical staff are exposed again and again, so they take these precautions every time.
A shorter half-life means a higher activity, so a bigger hazard at the start.
A longer half-life means the hazard lasts longer.
Reduce exposure with distance, time and shielding.

checks.q: Describe the difference between irradiation and contamination.
checks.a: Irradiation is the exposure of an object or person to radiation. Contamination is the unwanted presence of radioactive material on or inside an object or person.

checks.q: Explain why a source of alpha radiation inside the body is more dangerous than the same source outside it.
checks.a: Alpha radiation is stopped by skin, so outside the body the risk is low. Inside the body it is absorbed by tissue and is highly ionising, which damages cells and DNA.

checks.q: Two sources start with the same number of radioactive nuclei. One has a half-life of 2 years and the other 432 years. Which is the greater health risk at the start? Explain.
checks.a: The source with the half-life of 2 years. It decays faster, so it has a higher activity.

worked_example.question: Internal contamination of the human body means radioactive material is inside the human body. Explain how the risk from internal contamination is different to the risk from external irradiation by a source of alpha radiation.
answer_points: Alpha radiation has a low penetrating ability.
So externally, alpha radiation is stopped by skin, which is low risk.
Internally, alpha radiation is absorbed by living tissue or organs.
Alpha radiation is highly ionising.
Internal contamination causes greater harm to cells, tissues, organs or DNA.
worked_example.tip: Absorbed is accepted for stopped. Greater chance of cancer or mutations also scores.

items: Findings from studies into the effects of radiation on humans are published and shared with other scientists.
Other scientists can then check the findings. This is **peer review**.

worked_example.question: Exposing people to radioactive sources can be dangerous. Describe the dangers of exposure to radioactive sources and what can be done to protect hospital staff when they are working with radioactive sources.
answer_points: Dangers: radiation is ionising, it may cause cancer, it may destroy or kill cells, it can mutate DNA and it can burn the skin.
Protection: use tongs to carry the sources and use lead containers to store them.
Stay at a distance and use the sources for as short a time as possible.
Wear lead-lined protective clothing and give treatments from behind a shield or wall.
Wear a radiation badge (dosimeter).
worked_example.tip: This is a level-marked question. For top marks give a detailed explanation of both the dangers and the protection.

worked_example.question: In 1986, there was an accident when a nuclear reactor in a power station exploded. In the explosion, radioactive materials from inside the reactor were spread over the power station. Explain why workers at the power station were both contaminated and irradiated in the accident.
answer_points: Contaminated because radioactive material touched the workers or was breathed in.
Irradiated because the workers were exposed to radiation from outside of the body.
worked_example.tip: Keep the two ideas apart. A contamination answer that mentions radiation touching the workers does not score.

worked_example.question:
Radioactive isotopes that emit ionising radiation are used in hospitals.

State and explain two safety precautions necessary for the use of these isotopes in medical procedures.
answer_points: Reduce the exposure time, so a lower amount of radiation is absorbed.
Increase the distance between the source and the staff, so a lower amount of radiation reaches them.
Use shielding, such as walls or lead, so the radiation is absorbed and cannot pass through.
Any two precautions, each with its explanation.

blocks.text: (Supplement) Each precaution works by cutting the amount of radiation that reaches living tissue.

items: Reduce the time of exposure, so less radiation is absorbed.
Increase the distance between the source and living tissue, so less radiation reaches it.
Use shielding, so the radiation is absorbed before it reaches living tissue.
Radioactive materials are moved in sealed, lead-lined containers.
They are used for as short a time as possible and handled with tongs.
They are stored in lead-lined boxes, away from people.

worked_example.question:
A material called granite is used as a work surface in a kitchen. Thorium-232 is a solid and remains in the work surface. Radon-220 is a gas and is emitted from the work surface. Thorium-232 and radon-220 both emit alpha radiation.

Discuss the hazards due to the granite work surface when a person is working in the kitchen.

Refer to contamination and irradiation in your answer.
answer_points: Alpha radiation can cause cell mutation or cancer.
Alpha radiation is blocked by skin and by a few cm of air, so it is only dangerous inside the body.
Thorium stays in the work surface and cannot enter the body, so it can only cause irradiation.
Radon is a gas that can be breathed in, so it can cause contamination as well as irradiation.
worked_example.tip: Any three points score the 3 marks.

blocks.text: Radioactive waste stays dangerous for a long time. Disposing of it is a problem, and the risk is reduced in these ways.

items: Keep it in strong, sealed containers that will not rust or leak.
Bury it in a secure underground site, away from water and earthquakes.
Limit how often people handle it, and keep the site guarded.
